newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's exiled king to make pre-election visit.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's exiled king to make pre-election visit.

text.p: Bulgaria's exiled King Simeon is due to meet President Petar Stoyanov during a brief visit to his homeland on Tuesday and Wednesday that will take place just four days before parliamentary elections.
Simeon, who left Bulgaria as a child in 1946 and lives in Madrid, was invited for celebrations to mark the anniversary of the country's first constitution.

He will arrive in the town of Veliko Tarnovo on Tuesday afternoon, landing at a nearby airfield in a special aircraft, and will travel to Sofia on Wednesday for lunch with Stoyanov before returning to Madrid.
"He is always welcome to visit his homeland," Stoyanov's spokeswoman, Neri Terzieva, said on Monday, adding that the king had telephoned Stoyanov to seek his approval for the visit.
Officially the visit is non-political, and party leaders were reluctant on Monday to say whether they would meet Simeon.
The 1879 Tarnovo constitution, which marks its 118th anniversary this week, was the first to be drawn up in the newly independent state after 500 years of Ottoman rule.
The king will address the commemoration, then hold meetings with local and national political and civic organisations.
Inviting Simeon was an initiative of the Alliance for National Salvation, a coalition grouping the main monarchist parties and the ethnic Turks' Movement for Rights and Freedoms.

Simeon insists that he is the king of all Bulgarians and does not favour any one group, but he received leaders of the Alliance in Madrid last week and pictures of him with coalition leaders appear on their election posters.

Other monarchist movements are allied with the Union of Democratic Forces, which is expected to win a majority in Saturday's elections and is seen as more sympathetic to the monarchists' cause than the previous Socialist administration.

Now 59, Simeon fled Bulgaria in 1946 after the Soviet Army installed a puppet communist regime. He returned to Bulgaria for the first time for a three-week visit in May last year and was mobbed by an ecstatic flag-waving public.
At the height of demonstrations against the former Socialist government in January he added his voice to calls for early parliamentary elections as a way out of the crisis.
Simeon has never renounced his claim to the throne. As a Saxe-Coburg, he is related to other European royal families, including Britain's House of Windsor.
The balding, bearded monarch is respected even by republicans as a hard-working businessman who avoids the extravagant lifestyle of some royals.
